explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend! The psalmist asks the question in verse 1, then answers it right away: "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 121:2) No long pause, no guessing game. When the song asks where help comes from, the answer is already waiting.

I get why you'd pick it, friend. The psalmist does lift up their eyes to the hills, so they're right there in the picture. But the hills are only where the psalmist is looking. The psalm says, "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 121:2)

A king would sure make the song sound fancy! But no king shows up anywhere in these eight verses. The psalmist says, "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 121:2) The help comes from the LORD.

Yes, friend! The psalm says, "He will not allow your foot to slip…" (Psalm 121:3) Slipping is that sudden stumble that makes your stomach drop. I've done it on a floor dusted with flour, and my mustache went flying one way while the rest of me went the other. The psalm says the LORD won't allow it.

Tired feet are a real thing, friend, and I bet a good nap would fix them. But the psalm never says anything about tired feet. It says, "He will not allow your foot to slip…" (Psalm 121:3) The word is slip.
Wandering is a fair guess, friend. But that word isn't in this verse. The psalm says, "He will not allow your foot to slip…" (Psalm 121:3) So the word you're after is slip.

Not quite, friend. The psalm says the opposite, and it says it twice. First, "your Protector will not slumber." (Psalm 121:3) Then, "Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep." (Psalm 121:4) No slumber now and then, none at all.

That's right, friend! The psalm says, "your Protector will not slumber." (Psalm 121:3) Then it comes back and says, "Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep." (Psalm 121:4) It's not a nap here and there. The Protector doesn't slumber or sleep, period.

You got it, baker! "The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night." (Psalm 121:6) Shade is exactly what you want when the sun is beating down. And the psalm just said the LORD is the shade on your right hand (Psalm 121:5). That's the picture.

Wind is a fair guess, since it's one of those weather things you can't dodge. But it isn't in this verse. The psalm says, "The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night." (Psalm 121:6) The word that fits the blank is sun.

Rain makes sense if you're hunting for a weather word. But this psalm never mentions it. Right after the shade, the psalm says, "The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night." (Psalm 121:6) Sun is the one that fits. Think shade, not umbrella.

Not quite, friend. The psalm doesn't stop at sundown. It says, "The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night." (Psalm 121:6) Day and night are both covered, so this protection doesn't clock out when the day ends.
Right, friend! The psalm says, "The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night." (Psalm 121:6) It names the day and then it names the night. When the sun goes down, the psalm keeps going.
That's right, friend! The psalm says, "The LORD will guard you from all evil…" (Psalm 121:7) Look at that word all. The psalm doesn't pick and choose. It says all evil.
Not this time, friend. Evil is a heavy word, so I can see why this one might give you pause. But the psalm says, "The LORD will guard you from all evil…" (Psalm 121:7) It says guard, and it says all.

Yes, baker! "He will preserve your soul." (Psalm 121:7) It's right there after the line about guarding you from all evil. The verse names your soul, and the LORD is the One who preserves it. Nothing else fills that blank.
A house would be a handy thing to have preserved, friend. I'd sure want my bakery kept safe! But the verse doesn't say house. It says the LORD "…will preserve your soul." (Psalm 121:7)

Land sounds like a solid pick, friend, but it's not in this verse. I'd have bet my mustache on a few other words before that one. The psalm says the LORD "…will preserve your soul." (Psalm 121:7) Soul is the one that fills the blank.

That's it, friend! The psalm says the LORD will watch over your coming and going, "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 121:8) Now and forevermore. It's the last line of the song, and it doesn't have an end date.

Good thinking, friend, but the psalm doesn't put an end date on the watching. It says the LORD will watch over your coming and going, "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 121:8) Forevermore goes way past the end of any journey.

That sounds like a big promise already, and I see why you picked it. But the psalm goes further than that. It says the LORD will watch over your coming and going, "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 121:8) Forevermore isn't tied to a lifetime.
